NEWTON, Mass.--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Bright Horizons Family Solutions® Inc. (NYSE: BFAM), a leading provider of high-quality education and care solutions designed to help employers support employees across life and career stages, today announced financial results for the second quarter of 2021.
Second Quarter 2021 Highlights (compared to second quarter 2020):
Revenue of $441 million (increase of 50%)
Income from operations of $34 million (increase of 319%)
Net income of $19 million and diluted earnings per common share of $0.31 (increases of $18 million and $0.30, respectively)
Non-GAAP measures
Adjusted income from operations* of $34 million (increase of 25%)
Adjusted EBITDA* of $68 million (increase of 13%)
Adjusted net income* of $30 million and diluted adjusted earnings per common share* of $0.49 (increases of 13% and 11%, respectively)
“ I am pleased to report another solid quarter across all of our services, as we continue to make good progress in returning our business to pre-COVID-19 levels,” said Stephen Kramer, Chief Executive Officer. “ With full-time enrollment and back-up usage returning, and most centers re-opening by this fall, our recovery from the pandemic is on track. I continue to be inspired by our dedicated teachers and center operations leadership, who have been supporting children and families through these very challenging times, and likewise am proud of the strong client partnerships that have enabled the delivery of impactful solutions to families and learners over the past 18 months.”
Second Quarter 2021 Results
Revenue increased $147.7 million, or 50%, in the second quarter of 2021 from the second quarter of 2020, primarily attributable to enrollment increases in our open child care centers and the re-opening of our temporarily closed child care centers. While enrollment in our child care centers continued to improve during the quarter, our centers are still operating below pre-COVID-19 enrollment levels during this re-ramping phase. The increase in revenue in the full service center-based child care segment was partially offset by decreases in our back-up care services compared to the same period in the prior year. While we had gains from expanded back-up care client sales and increased utilization in traditional in-center and in-home care during the quarter, back-up care revenue decreased compared to the prior year as the second quarter in 2020 benefited from significant demand (primarily for self-sourced reimbursed care) during the early stages of the pandemic when other care alternatives were not available.
Income from operations was $34.0 million for the second quarter of 2021 compared to $8.1 million for the same period in 2020. The increase in income from operations reflects improved gross profit contributions in the full service center-based child care segment arising from higher enrollment as centers re-ramp and the re-opening of our temporarily closed centers, partially offset by reduced contributions from our back-up care services, which benefited in the second quarter of 2020 from increased demand during the early stages of the pandemic. Net income was $18.8 million for the second quarter of 2021 compared to net income of $0.4 million in the same 2020 period, an increase of $18.4 million due to the increase in income from operations, partially offset by a higher effective tax rate. Diluted earnings per common share was $0.31 for the second quarter of 2021 compared to $0.01 for the second quarter of 2020.

Daniel Houghton became the CEO of the popular travel publishing company, Lonely Planet, at just 24. The company wasn’t adapting to modern times and its future looked bleak. They needed someone young, someone who knew how to transition Loney Planet into the digital age, and someone who understood both media and technology. That’s when Houghton was tapped to lead the company. Under his leadership, the company modernized and developed a new generation of readers, and now has over 16.2 million followers on social media. Recently, Houghton stepped down as CEO and wrote the book Wherever You Go, which has just been released. I had the chance to sit down with him and ask about his time at Lonely Planet, his new book, and his future.
You became the CEO of Lonely Planet, one of the largest travel companies in the world, at just 24 years old. What was that like?
Well… the company didn’t exactly come with its own guidebook (laughs). It was really rough in the beginning. I come from a media background, but I had never had such responsibility before. It’s a huge company, but luckily, they have such a great team and it really became a group effort. But yeah.. there was a very steep learning curve for sure.
Did you enjoy your time there?
Oh, of course! I mean, it’s such an amazing company, it has a huge dedicated fanbase around the world, and travel is something I’m so passionate about. We hired people who loved the brand and loved travel, not people who were chasing money, and that made the entire company glow with such incredible energy.
You ended up stepping down from Lonely Planet, moved out to a farm in Tennessee and wrote a book. Explain how that happened.
Running a major company like Lonely Planet takes a lot out of you. It was an intense amount of travel and an intense amount of responsibility. We have a huge team that’s spread out all over the world. I spent about 200-250 days per year on the road, which I absolutely loved and it was amazing, but it also has a way of wearing you out. By the end, after the company had made such growth, I felt that I had left my mark. I had made some really good things happen and it just felt like it was the right time to start a new journey.
And unfortunately, then my dad got really sick, which I talk about in the forward of my book. So, I really wanted to be able to be close to my family. The farm thing came from me always wanting to live on a farm. I love woodworking, I love dogs, I love being outside, really, I just like a lot of old man things I guess! But yeah, with my dad being sick, I wanted some time off. I wanted to be with my family as much as I could. So now we all live in the same area and I can see them as much I want.

The Buccaneers didn’t play in Week 13. Which means that there was no reason for Buccaneers coach Bruce Arians to directly criticize (a/k/a be honest) or to passive-aggressively snipe at quarterback Tom Brady. Instead, Arians heaped praise on Brady.
“It’s been fantastic,” Arians told reporters when asked about working with Brady. “From day one, getting him here [and] watching him prepare and help young players get better. He’s a joy to coach and he’s a fantastic competitor. I love that about him. He’s been there and done it and he’s helped so many of our guys who haven’t [been there] believe that they can. That’s a huge part of it and I couldn’t ask any more out of him.”
Arians also praised Brady’s overall ability to show up and work every day, despite being 43.
“I don’t see any drop at all,” Arians said. “I’ve had some veteran guys that needed Wednesdays off and he’s not one of those guys. He’s amazing that way and how he takes care of himself. He’s helped a lot of young players learn about taking care of themselves also.”
Brady’s leadership and experience likewise was praised.
“There’s no doubt about it,” Arians said. “I’ve been very, very fortunate with some of the best quarterbacks that all have that. Every single one I’ve probably ever coached have had that ability. Peyton [Manning], Ben [Roethlisberger], Andrew Luck as a rookie was amazing. Tom [Brady], Timmy Couch, Kelly Holcomb — every one of those guys that were successful. When they got in the huddle, they had the ability to make everybody believe that this is the best play that’s going to be called and run. Then, walk off, work with guys, take them to the side, work with them and bring them along. All those great ones do it.”
Arians also didn’t take the bait when asked whether he’s frustrated with the offense’s inability to properly execute the scripted plays to start the game.

PYONGYANG, North Korea (AP) -- International Olympic Committee President Thomas Bach has met with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un in Pyongyang.
Bach told an Associated Press Television crew the two had a 30-minute formal meeting followed by 45 minutes of casual talking while watching a football match Friday afternoon at Pyongyang's huge May Day Stadium. He said Kim supports a plan to have North Korean athletes compete in the 2020 Tokyo Summer Olympics and the 2022 Beijing Winter Games.
Bach arrived in Pyongyang on Thursday to discuss development of sports in North Korea and the preparation of its athletes to qualify and participate in upcoming Olympics. He is the first foreign official to meet Kim since the North Korean leader returned from a summit in Beijing with Chinese President Xi Jinping.

The Golden Knights have boldly gone where no other U.S.-based NHL team has this season: Canada.

The Knights stayed awhile the last time they went to Canada.
They were in the NHL’s secure zone in Edmonton, Alberta, for 51 days for the 2020 postseason during their run to the Western Conference Final.

Opener Lizelle Lee smashed a blistering century before South African bowlers put up an outstanding effort to register an emphatic 113-run victory over debutant Thailand in the ICC Women’s T20 World Cup at the Manuka Oval in Canberra on Friday.
Electing to bat, the Proteas posted 195 for three, the highest team total in the tournament’s history, on the back of opener Lee’s 60-ball 101 and Sune Luus’ unbeaten 61. In response, Thailand was bundled out for 82 in 19.1 overs.
With the win, South Africa strengthened its grip on Group B as it gets ready to take on Pakistan on Sunday with the semifinals in sight. Thailand, which has a knack for nabbing early wickets, was gifted one when Dane van Niekerk (2) patted Ratanporn Padunglerd’s full toss to mid-on.
Lee, 10th in the ICC T20I batting rankings, dominated the scoring and slog swept Onnicha Kamchomphu for a 75-metre six. Thailand was forced to use seven different bowlers inside nine overs but none could withstand Lee's assault. She reached her 50 from 35 balls with a straight six.

24-year-old Luus, featuring in her fourth women’s T20 World Cup, then swung Chanida Sutthiruang’s full toss for six over fine leg. Lee came in without a half-century in nine international innings but glided towards a century in 59 balls, showing her touch with a late cut for four before bringing up a ton fittingly with a four.
Immediately after raising her bat to salute a jubilant South Africa dugout, she chipped a catch back to Suleeporn Laomi to end the partnership at 131.

Retired off-spinner Graeme Swann had bemoaned England's indifferent approach towards slow bowling before the five-match series started and his fears were confirmed after the touring side were handed a 4-0 drubbing.
The alarm bells would have been ringing when England's spinners were out-bowled in Bangladesh in October, where the side lost their first ever test against the hosts in a series regarded by many as an appetiser for the Indian leg of the trip.

Footwear supplier Pou Chen Corp (寶成工業) yesterday reported a net profit of NT$12.92 billion (US$443.18 million) for last year, down 1 percent from NT$13.06 billion in 2016, mainly due to higher expenses to expand and renovate its retail business.
Earnings per share were NT$4.38, down slightly from NT$4.43 in 2016, the company said in a statement.
Revenue totaled NT$278.63 billion, up 1.4 percent from NT$274.9 billion the previous year, while gross margin rose to 26.2 percent from 25.6 percent, the statement showed.
However, operating expenses over the period increased 6.5 percent to NT$56 billion, while operating profit decreased 4 percent to NT$17.7 billion.
Expenses rose because of an ongoing plan to expand its distribution channels and revamp some of its existing stores, the company said.
Pou Chen, the world’s largest branded athletic and casual footwear maker, operates its sportswear retail business in China through its Hong Kong-listed subsidiary, Pou Sheng International Ltd (寶勝國際).
Footwear manufacturing accounted for 70 percent of its revenue last year, while its retail business made up the remaining 30 percent.

Fans of Dave Chappelle's Comedy Central series Chappelle's Show will be surprised if they go to watch the stand-up comedian's sketch show on Netflix tonight. Why? Because Chappelle's Show has been removed from the streaming platform. The comedy series was released on both Netflix (and HBO Max) on November 1 — a huge move for the comedian who has had a multi-special deal with the streamer for years. Chappelle even mentioned this big release event during his opening monologue while hosting the most recent episode of Saturday Night Live.
But things have taken a turn in the weeks since Chappelle's Show hit Netflix and HBO Max. On Tuesday, Chappelle uploaded a video to his Instagram titled "Unforgiven." The 18-minute video appears to have been shot during a recent set of Chappelle's. Over the course of 18 minutes, Chappelle confirms he is the one who initiated the move to have Chappelle's Show removed from Netflix. He tied the show's removal from Netflix to ongoing issues with ViacomCBS and Comedy Central, who he claims did not pay him as part of the show's licensing contract.
In the video, Chappelle outlines his history of clashes with Viacom and why he left Chappelle's Show in 2005, saying, "If you are streaming that show, you are fencing stolen goods. They stole that (show) from me, they just took it," later going on to say, "I found out these people were streaming my work and never had to ask me or they never had to tell me. Perfectly legal because I signed the contract, but is that right? I didn’t think so."
Image via Netflix
Chappelle then offered thanks to Netflix for honoring his request to have the show removed, sharing with the audience, "(Netflix) agreed that they would take it off their platform just so I could feel better. That’s why I [work] with Netflix because they pay me my money, they do what they say they are going to do and they went above and beyond what you could expect from a businessman."
The veteran stand-up made an appeal to his audience in an effort to drive home his pain and disappointment with his treatment at the hands of Viacom: "So I’m not going to the agents, I’m coming to my real boss — I’m coming to you. I’m begging you — if you ever liked me, if you ever think there was anything worthwhile about me, I’m begging you, please don’t watch that show.

A standing COVID-19 vaccine clinic at La Palmera and a program to vaccinate homeless people are in the works, Corpus Christi and Nueces County officials said Thursday.
The La Palmera clinic will launch Tuesday and will be open Monday through Sunday during regular mall hours, public health director Annette Rodriguez said during the city and county’s weekly COVID-19 briefing.
People can pre-register or register on site, Rodriguez said. Officials hope to have at least 100 doses available every day.
To pre-register, visit cctexas.com/vaccineregistration or call 361-561-1101.
The clinic will be in the former Charming Charlie location near Grimaldi’s, Rodriguez said.
The mall is “a place that most of us might go anyway,” Nueces County Judge Barbara Canales said. “Whether you’re shopping or dining or getting your free, life-saving COVID-19 vaccine shot, it sounds like it’s a good day to be at La Palmera.
“La Palmera will be part of the many tools we have to fight back against this horrible disease.”
Homeless population
With shipments of Johnson and Johnson on the way, the city is working with providers of homeless services to identify the best way to reach that population, city spokeswoman Christian Cabazos said.
Unlike the two-dose vaccines by Pfizer-BioNTech and Moderna, the Johnson and Johnson vaccine requires only one dose. Experts say that makes it an ideal option for hard-to-reach populations.
“Your city and your health district are working to ensure that all populations have access to the vaccine,” Cabazos said.
Save Our Seniors
Registration for the Save Our Seniors vaccination program will open at noon Friday.

Bitcoin (CRYPTO: BTC) is the best known of the cryptocurrencies, and it's seen a rapid increase in price since the virtual coin was introduced. Many prominent financial experts have endorsed investing some money in Bitcoin, including Dave Ramsey and Suze Orman.
But even if putting some money into Bitcoin could potentially be a valid investment approach, you definitely shouldn't make it the centerpiece of your retirement saving efforts. Here's why.
You need to diversify, even with Bitcoin
Bitcoin has seen explosive gains since the virtual coin was created, and there's definitely an argument to be made that you could make a lot of money by investing in it.
But the problem is that its real-world utility is still currently limited, and it has a relatively short track record compared to many other assets you could invest in. It's impossible to know what the future holds for Bitcoin. And with the coins only having value because people believe they do, there's a very real chance that an investment in Bitcoin could end up being a loser over the long term.
While Bitcoin may be riskier than many other investments, such as index funds or stocks in established companies, that's not the only reason you shouldn't count on it to make you a retired millionaire. You shouldn't base your entire retirement portfolio around any single investment, whether Bitcoin or shares of Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL) or even an S&P 500 index fund.
That's because putting all of your eggs in one basket is simply too risky when it comes to retirement. Retirees cannot live on Social Security alone as it is meant to replace just 40% of your pre-retirement earnings. You need to have a sizable nest egg to cover the necessities without a lot of financial struggle, so you need a retirement portfolio that doesn't expose you to too much risk.
The best way to build such a portfolio is to invest in a wide mix of assets, including stocks, bonds, index funds -- and cryptocurrencies, if you're interested in buying them.

CHENNAI: Inscryption is really a nerdy puzzle-based deck-building game. It is based off a simple boardgame mechanic, which works surprisingly well as a videogame. What reeled me in, is its lore and the very peculiar, nightmare-esque aesthetic. I am in a cabin, the door is locked. The room is cloaked in darkness, and I only see a table, dimly lit by cursed candles that indicate my fate. On the other end of the table is a bearded stranger, with skeletal fingers and bright eyes. He immerses me into the illusion he has woven.
I am told that I am in a forest, in a caravan. The cards are my guardian creatures that help me struggle ahead. There are helpful witches, greedy hunters, and the occasional packrats. I must use the boons they give me to my advantage. I believe everything the stranger tells me. He challenges me to an insane card game. I must play, and I must win. Or I lose, and start from the beginning all over again.
To a person with no context, the cards would appear as though speaking a whole other language. But Inscryption does an excellent job of visually explaining the game mechanics.The game begins with a starter deck of woodland creatures. There are squirrels, and then other creatures. Squirrels could be sacrificed to give powers to the other creatures. The creatures would then attack the enemy, enough to tip over his damage scales — and make him lose.

The digital landscape has transformed drastically since the era of mainframes. Your company, like many others, has ridden each wave of technological advancement, from minis and microcomputers to the PC revolution, the dot-com boom with Sparcs, and the rise of databases like DB2, Oracle, and SQL Server. You embraced MPP, explored data cubes, and transitioned data to the intranet and internet.  VMware promised to control server sprawl, yet VM sprawl emerged. SharePoint became a fixture, and the allure of SaaS led you from Siebel to Salesforce.

Now, you're drowning in data. Your mainframe is a fragile relic, your SAN a costly black box offering little insight due to rampant VM and application sprawl.  Millennials advocate for "webscale" solutions like MongoDB, while Hadoop vendors promise magical insights from data lakes, introducing yet another storage technology to manage.

Enough is enough. This year, regain control of your data.  Here are 12 resolutions to guide your data strategy:

1. **Catalog Your Data:**  Knowing what data you possess is the first step. A comprehensive data mapping system is helpful, but the crucial element is a dedicated effort to locate and document all your data assets.

2. **Map Data Use:** Understand how your data is used by applications and its flow within the organization. Tracking data lineage and dependency, whether through software or manual effort, is vital.  Identify why data is kept, who uses it, and for what purpose. Define the data, its source system, and its usage.

3. **Understand Data Creation:**  Just as NASA’s reliance on incomplete data led to critical errors, understanding your data's origins is crucial. How are numbers derived?  This is an ongoing process, as new data sources constantly emerge, but it's essential for preventing avoidable disasters.

4. **Understand Data Flow:**  Mapping your organization’s data circulatory system—a comprehensive data flow diagram—is essential. This reveals inefficiencies ("black holes" and "miracles"), redundancies, and opportunities for optimization.  It also highlights where similar processes differ solely by technology stack, allowing for standardization.

5. **Automate Manual Processes:** Manual data manipulation in spreadsheets introduces latency and errors. By mapping your data flow, you can identify these manual processes and automate them, improving efficiency and accuracy.

6. **Embrace Machine Learning:**  Machine learning isn't magic, but it can automate pattern recognition and analysis. Identify at least one business process where machine learning can provide a demonstrable advantage. This is a practical step towards leveraging the power of data.

7. **Prioritize Natural Language and Voice Search:**  The future of data interaction is natural language and voice.  Making your data accessible through these modalities is no longer a luxury but a necessity to cater to evolving user expectations.

8. **Embrace Web Accessibility:**  Shift away from cumbersome desktop software.  Web-based applications offer greater flexibility, easier maintenance, and accessibility from anywhere.

9. **Prioritize Mobile Accessibility:**  Desktop computing is declining.  Ensure your data and applications are accessible on mobile devices to support the increasingly mobile workforce.

10. **Ensure High Availability and Distributability:**  Resilience is key.  Modern distributed databases designed for the cloud offer better uptime, scalability, and more affordable disaster recovery than traditional solutions.

11. **Consolidate Systems:** Simplify your IT infrastructure by consolidating redundant systems. This reduces complexity, maintenance costs, and improves overall efficiency.  While the business case may be challenging, the long-term benefits are significant.

12. **Visualize Data:**  Charts and visualizations make data more accessible and understandable.  Leverage visualization tools to communicate insights effectively.


By adopting these resolutions, you can transform IT from a cost center to a strategic asset, building a data-driven future for your organization.

These disclosures sparked outrage among journalists and press freedom advocates, prompting an internal review by the Justice Department's inspector general. Movie enthusiasts know that Hollywood releases its most prestigious films every December, just before the Oscar nomination deadline. Similarly, Broadway sees its most notable openings in the spring, right before the Tony nominations. This year's season is exceptionally crowded, with 18 shows—half of them musicals—debuting in March and April.

Last season was dominated by "Hamilton," which everyone anticipated would win the Tony for Best Musical. However, Barry Weissler, the producer of "Waitress," remained unfazed. 

"They were a massive hit, and some of our investors even begged us to delay for a season," Weissler says. "'Go to Chicago,' one of them suggested, 'and then come back.'"

Yet Weissler already had a theater and a cast in place, and despite not winning a single Tony Award, "Waitress" proved to be a profitable success. While Weissler took a gamble, other shows opted to sit out last season and are now opening before this spring's Tony deadline.

Scott Mallalieu, owner of GreatWhiteWay.com, a company that sells Broadway tickets to groups, believes that timing can dictate a show's success on Broadway. 

"The general rule of thumb is you don't want to open a show in the fall, because even with good reviews, it can be overshadowed by all the fresh new productions in the spring," he explains.

However, Mallalieu thinks this year might be an exception, as three hit musicals already opened in the fall: "Dear Evan Hansen," "Natasha, Pierre & The Great Comet of 1812," and "A Bronx Tale."

According to Jeremy Gerard, a theater critic for Deadline with four decades of experience covering Broadway, this leaves limited room for new shows to make an impact. He notes that many of these new productions are opening one day after another, vying for a portion of a relatively small audience.

"The producers know there's going to be a bloodbath," Gerard says. "The total size of the Broadway audience isn't highly flexible, and in fact, the numbers are decreasing. The grosses are going up due to insane ticket prices, led by 'Hamilton' with its $849 top ticket. So, the grosses are skewed, but the actual audience numbers are declining."

Nevertheless, in an industry where one in four Broadway shows fails, hope is ever-present, and producers employ various strategies to make their shows stand out. Sometimes, they hire a star, like Bette Midler in "Hello Dolly!" or adapt a popular movie, like "Groundhog Day" or "Amélie."

Yet some musicals, like last fall's "Dear Evan Hansen," manage to succeed without such strategies. This could also be true for this spring's "Come From Away," an original Canadian musical set in Newfoundland after September 11, 2001, when American airports were closed, and locals hosted 7,000 stranded passengers. Sue Frost, the lead producer of "Come From Away," acknowledges the risk.

"It was a title that no one understood; it was an ensemble piece with no stars, and people might label it 'the 9/11 musical'—so it was like three strikes!" Frost remarks.

*A Reuters Special Report*

At the NYPD police academy in Queens, New York, a police officer demonstrates a body camera during a news conference on the "Big Brother" pilot program involving 60 officers. The December 2014 initiative would later influence nationwide discussions on police accountability.

Civil rights advocates and law enforcement leaders are raising concerns about President Obama's $75 million proposal to equip local police departments with 50,000 body cameras. They emphasize that without robust oversight mechanisms, the technology's deployment could potentially undermine, rather than strengthen, public trust in law enforcement.

The proposal, which emerged following the Ferguson grand jury decision not to indict a white officer in the shooting death of an unarmed Black teenager, requires congressional approval. While it mandates department training and Justice Department guidance, questions remain about enforcement mechanisms.

## The Oversight Challenge

Barbara Arnwine, executive director of the Lawyers' Committee on Civil Rights, emphasizes the critical nature of accountability: "Without proper enforcement of disciplinary measures, body cameras become meaningless tools, especially in departments with poor track records."

Daytona Beach Police Chief Michael Chitwood's experience illustrates this concern. Chitwood advocates for strong federal guidelines that can withstand local political pressures and union influence.

The Police Executive Research Forum's recent study revealed that among 63 agencies using body cameras, one-third lack written policies governing their use. Critical questions remain unresolved:

- Privacy concerns in private residences
- Data storage duration
- Public access to footage
- Mandatory activation protocols

Research from Arizona State University demonstrates the impact of clear policies: officers are 20% more likely to activate their cameras when required by departmental policy.

The discussion reflects America's traditional tension between federal oversight and local control. While some lawmakers support body cameras in principle, they question federal involvement in local law enforcement.

State-level oversight may offer a middle ground. Several states, including Utah, Kansas, and Mississippi, are developing legislation to regulate body camera use. New Jersey's pending bill would require all state and local officers to wear cameras under attorney general guidelines.

In Ankara, Turkey, on May 5, 2016, Turkish Prime Minister Ahmet Davutoglu announced his decision to step down during a news conference at his ruling AK Party headquarters. This decision has raised concerns among German politicians about the future of Turkish governance, primarily due to the potential increase in President Tayipp Erdogan’s power.

Davutoglu is perceived in Europe as the more liberal face of the Turkish government. In contrast, Erdogan is heavily focused on establishing a powerful executive presidency, which critics argue could lead Turkey, an EU candidate, toward authoritarianism. Davutoglu had played a crucial role in negotiating a deal with Brussels to stem the flow of illegal migrants to Europe, a key factor that German Chancellor Angela Merkel hopes will bolster support for her conservatives ahead of a federal election next year.

Politicians from Germany's ruling coalition expressed their concerns on Thursday about the implications of Davutoglu's departure. Niels Annen, the Social Democrats' spokesman on foreign affairs, part of Merkel's coalition, told Reuters, "Erdogan will be able to push ahead with his plans to change the constitution now without opposition from his own ranks." He added, "In view of the prevailing climate of repression and the current debate about lifting the immunity of opposition lawmakers, this is bad news."

Erdogan's ruling AK Party has faced criticism for backtracking on media freedoms. It also aims to remove lawmakers' immunity from prosecution, a move seen as targeting a pro-Kurdish party in the Turkish parliament. Juergen Hardt, the foreign affairs spokesman for Merkel's conservatives, also expressed concern about Davutoglu's departure, stating, "Turkey will decide itself whether its future path leads to Europe or towards greater isolation."

German politicians have long followed Turkish affairs closely due to the significant Turkish community in Germany and the countries' trade relations. Germany, home to around three million people of ethnic Turkish background, is a vital trade partner for Turkey. The EU migrant deal with Turkey has been Davutoglu's project, yet Erdogan, frequently critical of the 28-nation bloc, has sometimes appeared to belittle his progress.

The migration issue remains a pressing concern for Germany.

A former police detective is behind bars after stealing thousands of pounds in cash seized from passengers at Heathrow Airport. Michael Harrington, 46, from Staines, worked at the airport as a Detective Sergeant with the Metropolitan Police, tasked with carrying out financial investigations and seizing unauthorised cash from those travelling in and out of the country. During his five years in the role, between July 2009 and July 2015, it is estimated that he stole between £75,000 and £83,000 from 16 victims, according to the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS).

In some instances, Harrington seized cash from victims and then falsely recorded that it had been given back after it was found to be lawful money. In others, he recorded the amounts seized to be less than they actually were, pocketing whole sums in the process. The disgraced former financial investigator was jailed for four-and-a-half years for 16 counts of theft at Southwark Crown Court on Wednesday (February 28).

Riaz Jakhura, from the CPS London’s Complex Casework unit, said: "Harrington took advantage of a number of passengers, including foreign nationals making their way through Heathrow Airport. He abused his position as a financial investigator for the police, contributing to significant stress and financial hardship for some of his victims. The overwhelming evidence against Harrington meant that he had no choice but to admit his crimes."

Two victims suffered financial loss when attending weddings abroad without the legitimate money they had planned to take with them. On one occasion, Harrington denied a victim the opportunity to have an interpreter present when confiscating legitimate money. He was caught when victims started to contact police about getting back the money seized, leading the police to Harrington. Harrington, who had been suspended from the Met Police pending the completion of the court case, admitted the thefts in October last year.

He had previously failed to turn up to an earlier sentence hearing, prompting a warrant for his arrest.

TALLAHASSEE, Fla. -- While hawksbill turtles are not the only marine turtles endangered by the destabilizing effects of climate change, a recent study by researchers at Florida State University indicates that this critically endangered species is particularly vulnerable.

The study, published in the journal PLOS ONE, was conducted by FSU's Department of Earth, Ocean, and Atmospheric Science. It suggests that projected increases in air temperatures, rainfall, and intense solar radiation could significantly reduce hatching success for hawksbills at several major nesting beaches.

Historically, Earth has experienced numerous climate shifts. However, researchers point out that today's rapid climate changes, combined with unrestrained human development, pose unprecedented threats to hawksbills and other marine turtles.

"Marine turtles have existed for millions of years and have adapted to significant climatic changes during that time," said Mariana Fuentes, Assistant Professor of Oceanography and co-author of the study. "In the past, they adapted by shifting their nesting grounds and seasons to align with more favorable conditions. However, increasing threats to nesting habitats from coastal construction, storms, and rising sea levels are jeopardizing their ability to adapt."

To assess the impact of climate change on hawksbill hatching success, FSU researchers analyzed over 5,000 nests from five Brazilian beaches, where most regional hawksbill nesting occurs. The team focused on five climatic variables—air temperature, rainfall, humidity, solar radiation, and wind speed—to develop a comprehensive model of the subtle effects of a changing climate on the sensitive incubation process.

"There is a lack of research on how climate change might affect hawksbills, especially this population," said Natalie Montero, a former FSU graduate student who led the study. "We chose to investigate the impact on hatchling production because significant changes in the number of baby marine turtles born can dramatically affect population stability."

As reptiles, marine turtles rely on external heat sources for body temperature regulation, making hawksbills and their relatives particularly sensitive to air temperature. This sensitivity is most evident in marine turtle nests, where extreme temperature fluctuations can influence egg incubation, dictate sex ratios, and determine hatching success.

For some marine turtle species, rising temperatures might not necessarily result in less successful incubation. For instance, a study by Montero and Fuentes published earlier this year showed that for loggerhead turtles on the temperate nesting beaches of North Florida, changing conditions might lead to potential short-term increases in hatching success by 1 to 7.6 percent.

However, the outlook for hawksbills is less promising. Montero and Fuentes found that rising air temperatures, coupled with increased rainfall and solar radiation, are projected to reduce overall hatching success at Brazilian nesting sites by up to 11 percent by 2100. Elevated temperatures may warm nests beyond the threshold for healthy incubation, while increased rainfall could saturate the soil and suffocate the embryos.

Even if the turtles manage to incubate successfully and hatch, they face the challenge of heightened solar radiation, which could heat the sand to the point of causing the nests to collapse—a major hazard for hatchlings as they make their way to the sea.

Although the future might seem bleak for this already dwindling species, Montero believes there is still time for humans to mitigate the impact.

"Humans can support marine turtles in numerous ways," she said. "Reducing coastal construction and protecting more coastal habitat will help ensure that both current and future nesting sites are available. It's also crucial to minimize human impact on dune structures and beach vegetation. Additionally, reducing trash and microplastics on the beach can create a higher quality nesting and incubation environment."

Maria A.G. dei Marcovaldi, Milagros Lopez-Mendilaharsu, Alexsandro S. Santos, and Armando J. B. Santos from the Fundação Pró-Tamar in Brazil contributed to this research. The study was supported by grants from the Sea Turtle License Plate Grants Program.

Japan’s consumption of green tea has been steadily declining, but a new breed of casual cafes specializing in the traditional brew is aiming to reverse this trend.  These cafes introduce customers to a wide variety of brands and unconventional serving methods, hoping to reignite interest in the beverage.  Pioneering this movement was Iemon Salon Kyoto, opened about a decade ago by the Suntory Group.  Designed to evoke the atmosphere of traditional Kyoto machiya townhouses, Iemon Salon offers a modern take on tea culture, pairing green tea varieties like sencha, hōjicha, matcha, and gyokuro with meals, sweets, and even tea-based cocktails and beer. Prices range from ¥518 for sencha and hōjicha to ¥928 for a cup of gyokuro.  The cafe's manager emphasizes their mission: “We hope to deliver the culture and spirit of Japan to the world through tea.”

Following in this innovative spirit is Tokyo Saryo, which opened in January in Tokyo's Sangenjaya district.  The location is fitting, as “Sangenjaya” translates to “three tea houses,” a name derived from the area’s history of tea establishments hundreds of years ago.  With its minimalist design featuring plaster walls and only nine seats surrounding the service counter, Tokyo Saryo encourages a focused tea-tasting experience.  The cafe offers rotating monthly menus featuring a selection of 25 tea brands.  Customers can sample two different brews of each tea: one at 70 degrees Celsius to highlight the tea's richness, and a second at 80 degrees Celsius to bring out its bitter and astringent notes.  Menus include detailed explanations of each brand's characteristics, catering to those less familiar with the nuances of green tea.  Sets are priced at ¥1,300 for two teas and sweets, or ¥800 for one tea and sweets.

A key element of Tokyo Saryo’s approach is the interactive experience.  Staff are available to discuss the teas, offering insights into production areas and flavor profiles.  This educational aspect draws in both young Japanese and international visitors, providing an opportunity to discover new favorite varieties. One overheard conversation illustrates this engagement: a customer remarked, “This tea tastes deep,” to which a staff member responded, “When you make tea at a low temperature you get the (taste of) amino acids.  Some people have told me that the color makes it look like broth.”  This emphasis on education and discussion, coupled with the unique brewing method—hand-pouring hot water over the leaves, similar to hand-drip coffee—sets Tokyo Saryo apart.  As one staff member explains, “We are happy to answer any questions about tea… so you can enjoy the depth of the (world of) tea.”

# Pilot Training Industry at Risk as Major School Faces Closure

The potential shutdown of Hamilton's prestigious L3 Airline Academy could herald a broader crisis in New Zealand's pilot training industry, which contributes $226 million annually to the economy.

L3 Airline Academy, renowned globally for pilot training excellence, faces likely closure in February 2021 due to border restrictions preventing international student entry. The academy has already implemented its own isolation facilities and received $836,000 in wage subsidies earlier this year.

Aviation NZ Chief Executive John Nicholson emphasized that his organization has been alerting the Government to the industry's challenges since May. "While L3 Academy isn't lost to New Zealand today, we need urgent government intervention to preserve both it and the broader international pilot training sector," he stated.

## Economic Impact

The international pilot training industry in New Zealand:
- Generates $51m in foreign exchange earnings
- Creates economic activity exceeding $226m, primarily in regional areas
- Employs over 380 staff, including 225 flight instructors
- Maintains assets valued at approximately $100m

## Current Situation

Despite 394 international students having signed up for training in September, none can enter the country, even those with visas. Nicholson suggests that allocating 440 visas over six months—matching the number granted to Russian fishermen—would be sufficient to sustain the industry.

International student pilots typically:
- Pay $80,000 in annual tuition fees
- Stay up to 18 months in New Zealand
- Secure airline employment upon completing training

## Strategic Opportunity

New Zealand's successful COVID-19 management and high-quality training programs have attracted increased interest from international airlines seeking alternatives to traditional training partners. "We have an unprecedented strategic advantage," Nicholson noted. "Never before have we had so many airlines interested in training their future leaders here."

However, domestic student training alone isn't economically viable, as international students typically comprise 70% of enrollment.

## Government Response

COVID Recovery Minister Chris Hipkins maintained that public health remains the top priority. While acknowledging the aviation sector's difficulties, he cited limited capacity in managed isolation facilities as a key constraint, particularly regarding essential workforce availability.

The Government has provided support through:
- $51m funding for sector recovery
- Levy removals
- Hibernation options for private tertiary establishments
- Entry allowance for 250 international PhD and postgraduate students

## Industry Perspective

Andrew Ridling, NZ Air Line Pilots Association president and Dreamliner captain, highlighted New Zealand's unique training environment: "Our challenging topography and dynamic weather patterns provide some of the world's most demanding and high-level pilot training, particularly valuable for Northern Hemisphere airlines."

The industry warns that L3's closure could trigger a domino effect among other training providers, potentially compromising New Zealand's position in the global aviation training market just as the sector prepares for post-pandemic recovery.

Out of these, 6,141 participants reported period symptoms, with the most common being abdominal cramps (83%), bloating (63%), and fatigue (61%). Other frequently noted symptoms included acne, headaches, mood swings, changes in appetite, lower back pain, and breast tenderness. Less common symptoms recorded were diarrhea, sleep disturbances, constipation, nausea, hot flashes, and ovulation pain.

A significant observation was that irrespective of race, ethnicity, age, or location, the frequency of symptoms was nearly uniform. Cramps, bloating, and fatigue were consistently reported as the most prevalent symptoms across the board, highlighting the impact these symptoms can have on any individual experiencing menstruation.

While these findings might seem apparent to those familiar with menstrual cycles, they underscore the inadequacies in current medical research concerning women's health.

Dr. Shruthi Mahalingaiah, a principal investigator on the study and an assistant professor at Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, emphasized the limited research in menstrual health despite advancements in cycle-tracking tools. Historically, menstrual health research has been marginalized, with women underrepresented in crucial large-scale studies.

A search for "menstruation" in PubMed between 2001 and 2018 yielded around 8,400 studies, significantly fewer than searches for other health issues like cardiovascular diseases or gender-specific conditions like prostate cancer or erectile dysfunction. The underrepresentation of women in clinical research, which persisted until Congress mandated their inclusion in trials in 1993, has led to a dearth of fundamental data and substandard healthcare for women.

Notably, wearables manufacturers have also contributed to this issue. While fitness trackers have been available since 2011, they were slow to incorporate features like cycle tracking. Apple and Ava are among the few companies engaging in clinical research specifically focusing on women's health.

The Apple Women's Health Study's initial results may not be groundbreaking, but the study's existence marks a positive step forward. Wearables offer a potential avenue to collect long-term data non-invasively, potentially opening doors for new discoveries and increased research in women's health. By involving a broad range of participants, this study has the potential to address the lack of foundational data in women's health.

Dr. Mahalingaiah stressed the need for further research on menstrual cycles, their implications for long-term health, and the impact of environmental factors on cycle characteristics. By establishing a comprehensive data set, studies like these can pave the way for advancements in women's health research and care.

# Neeraj Chopra's Journey to Tokyo Olympics: A Story of Comeback and Resilience

## The Triumphant Return
In a remarkable comeback, Neeraj Chopra threw 87.86m at the ACNW League Meet in Potchefstroom, South Africa, qualifying for the Tokyo Olympics by clearing the 85m mark. This achievement, coming after a 1.5-year hiatus, was particularly significant - the distance exceeded the 86.89m throw that won gold at the 2019 World Championships.

"I feel proud of making a strong comeback. Participating in a competition after 1.5 years and clearing the Olympic mark gives me immense satisfaction," Chopra says.

## The Injury Setback
The road to this comeback wasn't smooth. Following a stellar 2018, where he claimed gold at both Commonwealth Games and Asian Games and set a national record of 88.06 metres, Chopra began experiencing elbow pain in November 2018.

"I started feeling my injury back in November 2018. I continued to train, but was not having too many issues despite the pain. But it aggravated by April," he recalled. The condition worsened until he couldn't even lift a javelin, leading to surgery in May 2019.

## The Rehabilitation Journey
Post-surgery, Chopra underwent an intensive rehabilitation period, first in Mumbai and then at JSW's Inspire Institute of Sport in Bellary. He began with basic activities like cycling, gradually progressing to hand exercises and strength training.

"After surgery, I immediately started cycling, because I was unable to move my hand. Later, I started hand and strengthening exercises and slowly started gaining my strength. I kept myself motivated by setting a target for myself each day to do better than the previous day."

## World Championships Disappointment
Despite qualifying for the World Athletics Championships with an 83.90m throw in September 2018, Chopra had to withdraw due to his recovery. "I had trained really hard for the World Championships. It was constantly on my mind, whenever I was at the training. But injury ki wajah se sab gadbad ho gaya," he explained.

## The Path Forward
With the Olympic qualification secured, Chopra isn't resting on his laurels. He's already back in training, preparing for the Federation Cup and IAAF Diamond League in Doha in April, leading up to the Tokyo Olympics where he could become India's first track-and-field Olympic medalist since 1900.

"My target of qualifying for Tokyo is accomplished. From the next day onwards, I restarted my original training schedule. The preparations have begun for the Tokyo Olympics and for all the competitions that are on the road," he says.

## Mental Resilience
Throughout his recovery, Chopra maintained a positive attitude. "Everyone told me that injuries are a part of an athlete's life'. They told me not to worry too much about time off the track and just focus on my recovery."

"I believed I could qualify for Tokyo because I was having a good time at the training. Everything was working out and bhaari haath chal raha tha. So, I was expecting a good comeback. But the fact that I qualified on my first attempt, it makes me really happy," he concluded.

Car-buying consumers are at great risk after weather events like Hurricane Harvey and the threat posed by Hurricane Irma. They're at risk that flooded vehicles will eventually flood the market. The late Tom Zimmer, a former National Insurance Crime Bureau investigator and long-time source of mine, demonstrated for me three years ago how states will print salvage titles in the insurance companies' names -- and in a different color. "A regular Tennessee title is going to be green," he demonstrated. "Notice how the (Tennessee salvage title) is blue."

By law, when a flood drowns cars on a retail or auction lot, the lot must total out those vehicles in coordination with its insurance company and brand those cars' titles as salvage titles in the name of the insurance company. It also takes days, even weeks to secure a salvage title on a flooded vehicle. There's the flood itself, then the waiting to get a claims adjuster out to conduct an inspection, then the determination of loss and liability, then the generation of the title. "There's a gap of time between the actual incident and the branding of the title, so basically, you are unprotected at that point until those titles are branded," said Stan Norton, managing partner of City Auto and dealer member of the Tennessee Motor Vehicle Commission.

Bottom line, you should never buy a car without proof of a clean title. Period. If you insist on taking the risk of considering a car that has either a salvage title or no title at all, Zimmer said use your eyes -- and your nose -- to determine if it may be a flooded vehicle. "Are there artificial air fresheners in there that are probably covering up the odor of mold?" he said. He also said look for sand, dirt or silt traces in the upholstery, on the floorboard and around the interior. Chris Basso, public relations director for Carfax vehicle history reports, recommended before purchasing the car, have a reliable mechanic inspect the trunk, engine, and spare tire well for water or debris. "It's gone very well," Superintendent Kevin Wilson said. "Like with any new building, there's been a few growing pains, but we're really happy with the floorplan and the way that everything has evolved."

## Background and Need

The journey to the new school began in 2017 when voters approved a $17 million bond package. The construction was necessitated by an enrollment spike of more than 200 kids over just a couple of years.

According to Wilson, this put the district in an awkward position. They weren't big enough to support two full elementary schools, but their existing facilities were overcrowded. As a result, the previous elementary school (now the intermediate school) could only accommodate students up to the fourth grade, forcing fifth graders to attend classes with middle-school teenagers.

"We never really like having the fifth graders at the middle school, but we did it out of necessity," Wilson said. "Building the new school gave us an opportunity to bring them back into a more appropriate age group."

## Innovative Design

The district chose a pod floor plan that separates each grade level into different hallways. This layout limits traffic from other grades and fosters collaboration between teachers and students. Each pod includes collaboration spaces, allowing teachers to utilize an open classroom setup, employ technology, or coordinate small group projects.

Traffic safety experts have tried various strategies to combat speeding, as speeding-related crashes claim around 12,000 American lives annually. Initially, they attempted flashing signs to alert drivers of their speed, believing that drivers would slow down if they were aware of their speed. When this method proved ineffective, they deployed law enforcement officers to deter speeding, emphasizing the deterrent effect of severe penalties for speeding violations. Subsequently, hidden speeding cameras were installed on major roads to encourage cautious driving by creating uncertainty about when drivers were being monitored.

The latest approach in the ongoing battle against speeding involves placing a GPS device inside cars to incentivize drivers to maintain safe speeds. Researchers have discovered that a GPS device that monitors a vehicle's speed relative to the posted speed limit, coupled with a financial incentive, effectively reduces speeding behavior. In a study supported by the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, drivers were offered a $25 reward each week for safe driving, with penalties deducted for exceeding speed limits.

The experiment demonstrated significant reductions in speeding violations, particularly for drivers exceeding speed limits by nine or more miles per hour. The combination of rewards for safe driving and penalties for speeding violations proved highly effective in modifying driver behavior. The study revealed that some drivers even turned the incentive system into a personal challenge, further motivating them to comply with speed limits.

The success of this incentive-based approach suggests potential applications beyond research studies. Ian Reagan, a traffic safety researcher, envisions insurance companies offering similar tracking devices to policyholders interested in reducing their premiums. Unlike current rebate programs, these devices would provide real-time feedback to drivers, informing them of the financial implications of their driving behavior after each trip.

In conclusion, this innovative method of using incentives to promote safe driving behavior represents a promising advancement in traffic safety initiatives. By combining rewards and penalties, authorities aim to encourage drivers to adhere to speed limits and reduce the risk of speeding-related accidents. The evolving landscape of traffic safety strategies may soon see widespread adoption of such incentive-based programs by insurance companies and other stakeholders.

New Delhi: Following protests, the National Green Tribunal (NGT) clarified on Thursday that it had not declared the Amarnath cave shrine in the south Kashmir Himalayas a "silence zone."  A bench headed by NGT Chairperson Justice Swatanter Kumar stated that silence must be observed only directly in front of the ice stalagmite formation resembling the 'Shivalinga.'  A detailed order is forthcoming.

The NGT's clarification came after it had declared the shrine a "silence zone" on Wednesday, prohibiting religious offerings beyond the entry point.  The tribunal had previously suggested that establishing a "silence zone" around the shrine could help prevent avalanches and preserve the area's pristine environment.

The Amarnath cave shrine is a major Hindu pilgrimage site.  Covered in snow for most of the year, the cave is accessible to pilgrims only for a brief period during the summer.

The Vishwa Hindu Parishad (VHP), a Hindu right-wing organization, protested the NGT's initial order, calling it a "Tughlaki fatwa" (whimsical decree) and arguing that Hindus were not responsible for all ecological problems.

Conversely, environmental activist Gauri Maulekhi, whose petition led to the NGT's directions, welcomed the original order as "good and progressive."  She told PTI on Wednesday, "The Amarnath cave is situated in a fragile ecosystem.  These directions will make the Amarnath Yatra safer and more convenient for devotees, protecting the shrine from degradation and ensuring its preservation for future generations."

BAD AXE — A prosecutor involved in a sexual abuse investigation concerning priests from the Diocese of Saginaw has denied threatening the Diocese in a 2004 letter.

Mark Gaertner, a former Huron County prosecutor and current assistant prosecutor in Saginaw County, is collaborating with law enforcement on investigations into past sexual abuse of minors by priests in the Diocese.

Gaertner served as the Huron County prosecutor when Bad Axe Police investigated former Bad Axe Priest Jack E. Leipert following allegations of sexual abuse at Sacred Heart Church in 2000. Ultimately, the county chose not to press charges against Leipert despite a 21-year-old Caseville man accusing him of molestation.

The Diocese informed the Tribune this week that this complaint prompted Leipert's removal from the ministry in 2001. Erin Looby Carlson, director of communications for the Diocese of Saginaw, explained via email: "In 2001, it was determined that there appeared to be credible complaints involving the sexual abuse of minors against Jack Leipert from his earlier years in ministry."

Following the incident at Sacred Heart, Leipert was permanently removed from priestly duties and was prohibited from presenting himself as a priest.

Details of the investigation were reported by the Tribune in a May 2 article titled "Former Bad Axe Priest Investigated Locally for Alleged Sex Abuse." On Tuesday, Gaertner told the Tribune that the case against Leipert was not robust enough for a trial victory.

Efforts to gather evidence through a recorded conversation between Leipert and the alleged victim were unsuccessful due to technical failure and the alleged victim not asking all the questions provided by law enforcement.

Opioid use during pregnancy has risen dramatically, prompting new guidelines from the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) aimed at improving care for affected women and newborns.  According to the CDC, 7% of U.S. women reported using prescription opioids during pregnancy in 2019, with one in five of those women misusing the drugs. By some estimates, nearly 80 infants born with opioid withdrawal are diagnosed daily in the U.S., a number that has tripled in recent years.

These infants can experience symptoms such as tremors, fussiness, and diarrhea, and may be at risk for developmental delays, though other factors like alcohol use, poor prenatal care, or stress could also contribute, according to Dr. Stephen Patrick, lead author of the AAP report.

The new guidelines, released Monday, address the critical need for consistent and effective care.  “While we have been talking about the opioid crisis for years, pregnant women and their newborns seldom make it to the top of the heap,” said Patrick, a Vanderbilt University pediatrician. “Infants are receiving variable care and not getting connected to services.”

The AAP recommends that pregnant women with opioid addiction have access to medication-assisted treatment.  Two opioids, buprenorphine and methadone, are effective, but pregnant women often face stigma when using them, and prescribing doctors are scarce.  Furthermore, hospitals should have written protocols for assessing and treating opioid-affected newborns, a practice currently lacking in many facilities.

The AAP also emphasizes the importance of breastfeeding and other bonding practices, along with parent education and referrals to support services for affected newborns. These recommendations echo guidance from other medical groups and the U.S. government.

The pandemic may be exacerbating the problem, making access to treatment even more difficult.  "Getting into treatment may be getting even harder," Patrick said.

# Populist Leaders Endanger Human Rights, Warns Advocacy Organization

*UNITED NATIONS, Jan 12, 2017 (IPS)* - Human Rights Watch warned that populist leaders pose a dangerous threat to human rights, fueling and justifying intolerance and abuse worldwide, during the launch of their annual global report.

In its 2017 World Report, titled "Demagogues Threaten Human Rights," the advocacy group emphasized the rise of populist leaders and their rhetoric that undermines the global human rights system as one of today's most pressing challenges.

"The rise of populism poses a profound threat to human rights," said Kenneth Roth, Human Rights Watch's Executive Director.

Roth explained that populist leaders, who claim to speak "for the people," treat rights as an "impediment" and scapegoat minority communities to address public discontent and domestic issues.

"Trump and various politicians in Europe seek power through appeals to racism, xenophobia, misogyny, and nativism. They all claim that the public accepts violations of human rights as supposedly necessary to secure jobs, avoid cultural change, or prevent terrorist attacks," he added.

The report highlights how President-elect Trump's campaign embodied this politics of intolerance, addressing Americans' economic frustrations and security fears by proposing controversial policies, including:
- Mass deportation of undocumented immigrants
- Creation of a Muslim registry
- Use of torture

If enacted, these proposals risk not only violating human rights but also undermining the entire human rights protection system.

European leaders have exhibited similar populist tendencies. The UN Committee on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination noted that the UK's Brexit campaign employed "divisive, anti-immigrant and xenophobic rhetoric," prompting calls for officials to reject such discourse.

Despite some progress in relocating asylum seekers, British Prime Minister Theresa May maintained an anti-rights stance, criticizing "activist left-wing human rights lawyers" and seeking to exempt UK forces abroad from human rights law.

Human Rights Watch emphasized that undermining rights for some threatens rights for all. "You may not like your neighbors, but if you sacrifice their rights today, you jeopardize your own tomorrow," Roth cautioned. "In fact, disregard for human rights offers the likeliest route to tyranny."

The rise of Western populism and muted response to violations has emboldened leaders worldwide:

- China's Xi Jinping has led an unprecedented crackdown on dissent
- Turkey's Erdoğan has crushed political and media opposition
- Burundi's Nkurunziza announced withdrawal from the International Criminal Court
- Syria's Assad and Saudi Arabia's Mohammad Bin Salman continue civilian attacks with apparent impunity

Akshaya Kumar, Human Rights Watch's Deputy UN Director, noted that populist leaders now embrace rather than shy away from anti-rights rhetoric. Examples include:

- Hungary's Viktor Orbán's open Islamophobia and anti-refugee policies
- Philippines' Rodrigo Duterte's explicit endorsement of extrajudicial killings

To combat these trends, Kumar advocates targeting enablers of rights abuses, including financial backers and arms suppliers. Recent successes include Canada's 2006 prohibition of LTTE fundraising and the U.S.'s 2016 suspension of arms sales to Philippine police.

The report emphasizes the crucial role of civil society organizations, media, and governments in defending human rights, particularly as some leaders "buried their heads in the sand, hoping the winds of populism will blow over."

Ultimately, the public bears responsibility for addressing populism and promoting human rights. As Roth concluded, "Values are fragile... A society's culture of respect for human rights needs regular tending, lest the fears of the moment sweep away the wisdom that built democratic rule."

Rainy Roth, a children’s ministry leader in her Montana church, volunteers as a crisis counselor with Crisis Text Line.  From her computer in a small town (population 943), she connects with people, primarily under 25, who are struggling with a variety of issues. This work, she finds, intertwines with her role at church, as both involve supporting and nurturing young people.

As a crisis counselor, Rainy completed a rigorous 34-hour training program, covering topics from active listening techniques to dealing with self-harm, suicide, depression, bullying, and gender/sexual identity.  This prepared her for the challenging but rewarding work ahead.

Rainy’s motivation stems partly from her own childhood experience with undiagnosed anxiety.  In the 1960s, mental health awareness was limited, and her struggles were misunderstood.  Now, she finds solace in being able to tell someone, “I get it,” offering understanding and validation she lacked as a child.

While she helps texters with various challenges, Rainy finds the “active rescues” – intervening when someone expresses imminent plans to harm themselves or others – particularly impactful.  Knowing she played a role in getting someone immediate help is profoundly rewarding. “It’s not only about saving lives,” she explains, “it’s also about letting these individuals know that people care.”

A simple phrase, “You matter,” carries surprising weight for many texters.  Rainy frequently hears, “Wow, I have never heard that before!”  These two words offer reassurance and a sense of belonging, countering negative thoughts and feelings.

The connection she forms with texters is deeply fulfilling.  Hearing them acknowledge her words brings a sense of comfort and, in a way, heals a part of herself that struggled for so long with unnamed fear and anxiety.  Being able to identify with their experiences allows her to help them understand that their feelings are valid and that there is hope for change.

Rainy believes she has become a better and healthier person through her work as a crisis counselor.  Her compassion, combined with the skills she gained through training, allows her to offer support and reassurance, letting those in crisis know that things will ultimately be okay.

Today, the Northern Virginia Transportation Commission (NVTC) approved the release of the Report on Virginia’s 3% Cap on the Growth in Operating Assistance Payments to the Washington Metropolitan Area Transit Authority (WMATA) to the Virginia General Assembly, as mandated by law.

In 2018, the General Assembly established a 3% cap on the growth of Virginia’s annual operating subsidy to WMATA. This measure was part of Virginia's commitment to providing a dedicated source of capital funding. If, in any given year, the approved WMATA operating subsidy increase for Virginia surpasses 3% (excluding legislative exemptions), the legislation requires the Commonwealth Transportation Board (CTB) to withhold 35% of the state funding allocated to NVTC. This funding serves as capital and operating assistance to help local jurisdictions meet their financial commitments to WMATA. In 2020, the General Assembly directed the formation of NVTC’s 3% Cap Working Group to examine the cap's effectiveness and consider whether additional exemptions should be included.

The NVTC’s 3% Cap Working Group, consisting of experts and stakeholders from Northern Virginia’s localities, determined that the 3% cap is a useful tool for managing the growth of Virginia’s operating subsidy. With only two years of WMATA budget development since the cap's implementation, the Working Group recommends the following:

- No changes should be made to the existing 3% cap legislation at this time.
- No additional exclusions should be considered.
- NVTC should collaborate with the Department of Rail and Public Transportation to clarify existing state policy guidance regarding the current legislative exclusions to the cap.
- NVTC should continue to explore potential modifications to Virginia’s 3% cap legislation, with the scope and timing of such efforts to be determined by the Commission.

The city, according to Isabel Gonzalez-Webster of Worcester Interfaith, must ensure solid policies are in place to make body cameras a tool of trust between the police and the community. She urged the city to go beyond the state task force recommendations and set a high standard for body camera usage, emphasizing the need to balance transparency with privacy considerations.

Daniel Nakamoto from the state Executive Office of Public Safety and Security discussed the state's efforts to assist local departments in developing body camera programs. Rahsaan Hall of the ACLU stressed the importance of community engagement in shaping body camera policies, emphasizing transparency and privacy considerations. Scheduled listening sessions in various districts will provide an opportunity for community input on the issue.

The simultaneous arrival of a new Little Women film and a television series about Emily Dickinson has sparked a conversation about how we reimagine the lives of girls and women of the past.  Both projects offer fresh takes on 19th-century New England, specifically the 1860s, and the interior lives of young women constrained by societal expectations.  This shared context makes comparing the two projects particularly compelling.

Greta Gerwig's adaptation of Louisa May Alcott's *Little Women*, boasting a star-studded cast, promises a modern sensibility while remaining faithful to the source material.  The trailer showcases a dynamic portrayal of the March sisters, highlighting their ambition, talent, and struggles against societal limitations. Gerwig’s use of Alcott’s own letters, as evidenced by Jo’s impassioned speech about women’s minds and souls, demonstrates a commitment to capturing the spirit of Alcott's vision.  This approach suggests a balance between historical context and contemporary resonance, aiming to make the story feel relevant to a modern audience.

In contrast, Apple TV's *Dickinson*, starring Hailee Steinfeld, takes a more radical approach to its subject matter.  The trailer presents a rebellious, almost anachronistic Emily Dickinson, challenging the historical image of the reclusive poet.  This Dickinson embraces fame, plays air guitar, and seeks out passionate encounters.  While visually compelling, this portrayal raises questions about historical accuracy and the potential prioritization of "Girl Power" aesthetics over the nuances of Dickinson's complex inner life.  The series appears less concerned with faithfully representing the poet and more interested in using her name as a hook for contemporary audiences.

The different approaches of these two projects raise important questions.  In a media landscape saturated with reboots and adaptations, how much creative license is acceptable?  Is historical accuracy essential, or can these reimagined stories offer valuable new perspectives?  *The Favourite*, for instance, demonstrated that historical accuracy isn't always necessary for a compelling and successful narrative.

Both *Little Women* and *Dickinson* are derived from rich source material. Alcott’s *Little Women* is semi-autobiographical, reflecting her own experiences growing up.  Dickinson's poetry, though often interpreted through the lens of her secluded life, offers glimpses into a passionate and imaginative mind.  These projects, along with previous adaptations of both stories, highlight the enduring fascination with these figures.

Ultimately, the success of these projects will depend on their execution.  Trailers, designed to generate excitement and anticipation, don't always reflect the final product.  Whether these adaptations will resonate with audiences and offer meaningful insights into the lives of these women remains to be seen.  However, their very existence underscores the continued relevance and richness of the female experience, past and present.  The territory of girlhood, as these projects demonstrate, continues to offer fertile ground for exploration, even if faithfulness to historical detail sometimes takes a backseat to creative interpretation.

**MOSCOW (AP)** — Russia's foreign minister has accused Britain and the United States of spreading "lies and disinformation" about the poisoning of a Russian ex-spy in England, asserting that East-West tensions are worse now than during the Cold War. 

Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov denounced the British accusations on Monday as a "mad and horrible provocation," asserting that Russia had no motive to attack Sergei Skripal, a former double agent, and his daughter Yulia, who were poisoned on March 4 in Salisbury, England. Lavrov argued, "If there were any gripes against the man, he wouldn't have been swapped," referencing Skripal's release in a 2010 spy swap from a Russian prison where he was serving time for spying for Britain.

Lavrov criticized Britain's claim that there was no plausible alternative explanation for the poisonings, suggesting that British intelligence agencies could have been involved. He further speculated that the case was a distraction from the British government's troubled Brexit negotiations, stating, "It could also be advantageous to the British government, who clearly find themselves in a difficult situation having failed to fulfill their promises to voters over Brexit."

British officials have previously dismissed similar allegations from Russia. Nevertheless, Russia has called a meeting of the international chemical weapons watchdog for Wednesday to discuss the case, seeking details on its cooperation with Britain in the investigation. 

Alexander Shulgin, the Russian representative at the Organization for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons (OPCW), emphasized on Monday the need for an "open, thorough and unbiased investigation" with Russian experts' participation. He cautioned that Moscow would not accept the agency's conclusions unless Russian experts were involved.

British authorities have invited OPCW experts to take chemical samples from Salisbury and analyze them.

# Athens Olympics: A Decade Later - Promise, Pride, and Missed Opportunities

## The Dream Begins
After failing in a bid to host the centennial Olympics in 1996, Greece, founder of the ancient and modern Olympics, was awarded the 2004 Games after defeating favorites Rome. The announcement sparked jubilant celebrations, with the Greek delegation, including then-minister George Papandreou, erupting in joy. The moment was so significant that a DJ-remixed version of the announcement was even released as a single.

## From Euphoria to Reality
However, the initial euphoria quickly gave way to challenges. Athens wasted the first three years of its seven-year preparation period, prompting a warning from the IOC in 2000 to accelerate its efforts or risk losing the Games. This led to a frenzied construction period, with crews working three shifts daily to complete venues just weeks before the opening ceremony.

The Games ultimately cost Greece an estimated $11 billion—double the initial projections. New infrastructure emerged across Athens: trams, highways, and gleaming Olympic venues appeared alongside the city's existing architecture. Banners proudly proclaimed "Welcome Home" during the Games.

## A Decade of Decay
Today, ten years later, the legacy of the 2004 Olympics tells a different story:

- The once-gleaming Olympic venues now largely stand abandoned
- The former canoe and kayak venue has dried up, with spectator seats torn out
- At the Olympic rowing center in Marathon, stray dogs roam among overgrown weeds
- Many venues are used only occasionally for non-sporting events like conferences and weddings

## The Economic Impact
For Greeks who once swelled with pride, the Games have become a source of frustration as the country struggles through:
- A six-year depression
- Record unemployment
- Rising homelessness and poverty

While the Hellenic Olympic Committee maintains that the Games' €8.5 billion cost didn't significantly contribute to Greece's €360 billion debt crisis, critics argue differently.

Drivers in the UK can face penalties for reversing further than necessary.  The Highway Code states that "you must not reverse your vehicle further than necessary," a rule reinforced by Section 106 of the Road Vehicles (Construction and Use) Regulations 1986. This law stipulates that reversing should only be done as far as required for the safety and reasonable convenience of vehicle occupants and other traffic.  Therefore, if a police officer deems a driver has reversed excessively, they could be charged with driving without due care and attention, leading to a £100 fine and three penalty points on their licence.  This is in addition to the existing penalties for reversing on a motorway or dual carriageway, which carries a maximum fine of £2,500 and three penalty points.
